title: Retail Replacement Sourcing
name: Retail Replacement Sourcing
metaTitle: Retail Replacement Sourcing for San Francisco 1031 Exchanges
metaDescription: Retail replacement sourcing for San Francisco 1031 exchanges, tracking ground-floor recovery citywide against steadier Burlingame and Millbrae storefront corridors.

sections.html: Ground-floor retail in San Francisco has been a slower recovery than most other asset classes, and anyone who's managed a mixed-use building through a long storefront vacancy knows what that actually costs beyond lost rent. A dark ground floor changes foot traffic for the tenants above it, changes how a building reads to a prospective office tenant touring the lobby, and changes insurance and security costs in ways that don't show up on a simple retail rent roll. Pricing a retail replacement candidate correctly means accounting for all of that, rather than only the quoted cap rate.

sections.heading: Where the Ground-Floor Recovery Actually Stands Block by Block
sections.html: The recovery isn't uniform, and treating it as a single citywide trend line is how buyers misprice a candidate. Some corridors have backfilled with service and food tenants that pay less than the pre-vacancy retailer but sign longer terms, while other blocks are still carrying storefronts dark for a stretch that would have been unusual before 2020. We walk the block ourselves, rather than relying only on the comp set, before recommending a candidate, since foot traffic and adjacent vacancy tell a story a spreadsheet comp can't.

sections.heading: Burlingame and Millbrae Offer a Steadier Comparison Point
sections.html: Retail corridors in Burlingame and Millbrae haven't carried the same vacancy swings as the city's ground-floor stock, giving investors a useful comparison for what a fully stabilized small-format retail asset actually performs like right now. That doesn't make them automatically the better buy, since cap rates in those corridors have compressed to reflect the stability, but they're a useful benchmark against a discounted city candidate that's pricing in a recovery that may or may not fully happen. Comparing the two side by side is often more useful than evaluating either in isolation.

sections.heading: What We Verify Before a Retail Candidate Reaches the List
sections.html:
• current occupancy on the ground floor versus the building's historical baseline
  • tenant mix and whether it leans toward service, food, or traditional retail
  • co-tenancy and exclusive-use clauses that could limit backfill options
  • storefront and signage condition against local permitting requirements
  • percentage rent structure, if any, and how it's tracked and audited
  • parking availability for customers, since it varies more than most listings disclose

sections.heading: Daly City's Neighborhood Retail Runs on Different Fundamentals
sections.html: Neighborhood retail in Daly City trades more on proximity to residential density and daily-needs tenant mix than on the recovery narrative driving downtown corridors. A grocery-anchored or service-anchored strip there behaves more like a defensive holding than a recovery play, which makes it a different kind of candidate entirely, not a lesser one. We underwrite it against its own daily-needs demand driver rather than against the city's ground-floor recovery timeline.

sections.heading: Pricing a Recovery Candidate Against a Stabilized One
sections.html: The real decision an investor is making is whether to buy the discount priced into a still-recovering ground-floor asset or pay the premium for a stabilized corridor that isn't likely to get cheaper. We lay both paths out with the same underwriting rigor rather than steering toward whichever one happens to be easier to source that week. Neither path is inherently the right answer, and the honest comparison depends on how much vacancy risk an investor actually wants to carry.

faqs.q: Why does ground-floor retail vacancy affect a mixed-use building beyond lost rent?
faqs.a: A dark storefront changes foot traffic for tenants above it and can affect how the building presents to a prospective office tenant touring the lobby, along with insurance and security costs that don't appear on a simple retail rent roll and are easy to underestimate from the outside.

faqs.q: Is the ground-floor retail recovery happening evenly across the city?
faqs.a: No. Some corridors have backfilled with service and food tenants on longer terms, while other blocks are still carrying storefronts vacant for a stretch that would have been unusual before the pandemic. We check block by block rather than relying on a citywide average.

faqs.q: Are Burlingame and Millbrae retail corridors automatically a better buy than city retail?
faqs.a: Not automatically. Cap rates there have compressed to reflect their stability, so they serve better as a benchmark for what stabilized retail performs like than as a guaranteed better value.

faqs.q: How is Daly City neighborhood retail different from downtown recovery-play retail?
faqs.a: It trades on proximity to residential density and daily-needs tenant mix rather than a recovery narrative, making it a defensive holding rather than a bet on ground-floor vacancy filling back in.

faqs.q: What should be checked on percentage rent clauses in a retail rent roll?
faqs.a: How the reported sales figures are tracked and audited. A percentage rent clause that looks like upside on paper is only worth what the audit trail behind it can actually verify.

faqs.q: How does a co-tenancy clause affect a retail replacement candidate?
faqs.a: It can allow a tenant to reduce rent or terminate early if another tenant in the same building or center closes, which turns a single vacancy into a compounding risk if the lease isn't reviewed carefully before identification, especially in a corridor still working through its own recovery.

faqs.q: Why does signage and storefront condition matter for retail underwriting?
faqs.a: Local permitting requirements for signage changes can add real delay to backfilling a vacant storefront, so we check the current condition and permitting history rather than assuming a new tenant can simply install new signage on the seller's timeline. That delay directly affects how quickly a discounted, still-recovering asset can actually turn its vacancy around.
